title: Property-dependent material times
authors: Aude Y. Amari, Lorenzo Costigliola, Jeppe C. Dyre
abstract: We analyze simulations of physical aging following large temperature up-jumps from equilibrated, slowly relaxing states. Specifically, we consider up-jumps from temperatures T=0.43 and T=0.37 to T=0.48 in a binary Lennard-Jones mixture. The Tool-Narayanaswamy (TN) concept of a universal material time was recently shown to become less effective in rationalizing the aging response for such large jumps [Amari et al., Phys. Rev. E 113, 045411 (2026)]. Here, we investigate whether the performance of the TN formalism can be improved by assigning a separate material time to each observable. We examine the potential-energy time-autocorrelation function, the self-intermediate scattering function, and the time-dependent mean-square displacement. As part of this study, we perform a detailed analysis of the extent to which the triangular relation, a necessary condition for the existence of a material time, is satisfied. We find that, for all three properties, the best data collapse is obtained when each property is parameterized by its own material time. The degree of improvement varies considerably among the observables, however; it is most pronounced for the mean-square displacement.
summary: This paper analyzes the aging dynamics of a binary Lennard-Jones mixture following large temperature jumps. The authors test if assigning a unique material time parameterization to different physical observables (like MSD or ISF) improves the description compared to using a single universal time scale. They find that individual material times provide the best data collapse for all measured properties, highlighting the complexity of relaxation in glassy systems.
main_problem: The study investigates physical aging dynamics following large temperature up-jumps, specifically testing if parameterizing different observables by their own material time improves the effectiveness of the Tool-Narayanaswamy (TN) formalism.
main_result: For all analyzed properties—potential energy autocorrelation, ISF, and MSD—the best data collapse is achieved when each observable is parameterized by its unique material time. The improvement is most pronounced for the mean-square displacement.
method: The authors analyze two-time correlation functions ($C_{uu}, F_s, \langle\Delta r^2angle$) and test their consistency with a generalized 'material time' concept derived from satisfying necessary conditions like the triangular relation.
model_or_system: The simulations are performed on a binary Lennard-Jones (LJ) mixture (mBLJ system), modeling structural relaxation in a glassy or amorphous material context. The analysis focuses on non-equilibrium dynamics far from equilibrium.
key_observables: Potential-energy time-autocorrelation function ($C_{uu}$), A-particle incoherent intermediate scattering function ($F_s$), and A-particle mean-square displacement ($\langle\Delta r^2angle$).
important_parameters: Temperature jump magnitudes (e.g., $0.43 	o 0.48$); the material time parameterization constant 'a'.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that defining a separate material time for each observable can improve data collapse, even when standard universal material time concepts fail during large temperature jumps.
figures_summary: Figures show simulation results for $C_{uu}$, $F_s$, and $\langle\Delta r^2angle$ following up-jumps. Later figures illustrate the collapse of these two-time functions when plotted against differences in their respective material times.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes aging dynamics by comparing the effectiveness of universal vs. property-specific material time parameterizations for three key observables, confirming that individual material times yield superior data collapses, especially for MSD.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium relaxation in glassy systems using advanced concepts like 'material time,' which is highly relevant to understanding structural arrest and slow dynamics in complex materials studied by AMO physicists.
